source.title: The Blessing and Curse of Dimensionality in Safety Alignment
source.citation: Rachel S. Y. Teo et al., 2025
source.authors: Rachel S. Y. Teo; Laziz U. Abdullaev; T. Nguyen

record.tranche_reason: The study computes difference-in-means directions and evaluates ActAdd and directional ablation on aligned chat/instruct models, reporting refusal and safety outcomes on harmful prompts. This directly applies the direction-based interventions and behavioral measures described in the original study.
record.gate_note: The PCA visualizations and probe accuracies about safety linearity are not rows here: they do not measure refusal behavior under the direction interventions. The paper also reports results for its newly trained FJLT and Bottleneck defenses; those defense results are not cataloged as independent tests of the claim’s direction intervention. Rows below retain the unmodified baseline models’ reported attack outcomes and ActAdd benign-prompt refusal outcomes.
record.test_reason: Mainly a defense paper, but it reruns the Arditi et al. difference-in-means attacks on three unmodified safety-tuned models. These are directional ablation at all layers and positions, and ActAdd. It reports refusal (substring) and Llama Guard 2 safety scores on JailbreakBench, AdvBench and HarmBench, plus refusal on harmless Alpaca prompts. Same method and measures as the original, on Llama2-7B-Chat, Gemma-1.1-7B-IT and Qwen2-7B-Instruct. The FJLT and Bottleneck defense results are the authors' own method and are not tests of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors argue that linear concept structure, including safety, emerges with larger hidden dimension, making models open to linear steering jailbreaks (ActAdd, ablation). Projecting representations to lower dimension (FJLT, Bottleneck) with fine-tuning resists these attacks while keeping alignment. Bottleneck preserves utility better than FJLT. Effectiveness varies by model, and the defenses do not help against GCG.
record.recipe_differences: The study follows the difference-in-means direction procedure and evaluates ActAdd and directional ablation with refusal and safety metrics. It selects candidate layer/position vectors using validation behavior; for ablation, the selected direction is projected out across layers and positions. The ActAdd intervention is evaluated as a jailbreak rather than as a systematic test of all harmless-prompt steering strengths.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack outcome varies by model and benchmark: Gemma retains more refusal/safety under ActAdd than Llama2 and Qwen2; on harmless prompts, ActAdd refusal scores differ by model (Llama2 1.00, Gemma 0.62, Qwen2 0.91).

fits_no_version.finding: Low-dimensional projection defenses (FJLT on one attention head; a linear bottleneck after layer 0), fine-tuned on refusal data, keep refusal at about 0.73-1.00 under ActAdd and ablation on Llama2 and Gemma (Table 12). Qwen2-Bottleneck stays weak (0.08-0.66). Plain refusal fine-tuning alone raises Llama2 refusal under ablation from 0.07 to 0.47. The defenses lower linear-probe accuracy for harmful vs benign prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Constraining representation dimensionality during fine-tuning makes difference-in-means refusal steering and ablation attacks ineffective while keeping refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear separability of concepts (emotion) appears only in models above about 2,000-3,000 hidden dimensions (Figures 2-3). Baseline Gemma-1.1-7B-IT harmful/benign prompts separate only along PC3.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear concept directions used for steering emerge with hidden dimension.

record.code_released: Source code is stated to be in the supplementary material; no URL stated.
record.problems: The intervention direction is selected from candidates using validation behavior, and the reported attack evaluations use finite benchmark prompt sets. The main attack tables do not report uncertainty for the baseline attack results. Evidence about preserving utility comes from separate defense models and selected utility benchmarks; the paper does not establish that the original single-direction ablation preserves general capability.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted ActAdd and ablation results for the paper’s fine-tuned, FJLT, and Bottleneck variants from Table 12, which would add many condition-specific rows; the catalog retains the unmodified baseline models to document attack behavior on the safety-trained models named by the claim. Also omitted benign-prompt perplexity values from Tables 1 and 2 because they do not directly measure whether harmless requests are refused.

untested.parts: Preservation of general capabilities after ablation or addition on the unmodified models. Utility (Table 13) is reported only for FT/FJLT/Bottleneck models, never for the attacked baselines. Whether a single direction is the sole mediator.
No weight-edit or abliterated released model evaluated.
No test of whether other jailbreaks (e.g. GCG, Table 14) act by suppressing the direction. The defenses are dimensionality-reducing architectures plus fine-tuning, not training against the ablation.
Not tested. The probes classify harmful vs benign prompts, not refusal.

missing.what: ActAdd on unmodified Qwen2-0.5B-Instruct: harmful refusal 0.01, safety 0.27, harmless refusal 0.91. This is a V1 result on a small model with weaker linear safety structure.

Unattacked baseline scores for the three models on JailbreakBench/Alpaca (refusal 0.97/0.92/0.99; harmless refusal 0.00/0.00/0.01). These are already used as baselines, but no AdvBench/HarmBench unattacked baselines exist.

record.verdict_notes: The study does not challenge the direction finding; it takes it as the threat model. Baseline-model results replicate V1 on new model versions. The operation label for ActAdd on harmful prompts is ambiguous in the paper: the text says the direction is added, yet harmful refusal drops. The Background section also oddly says ablation 'induce[s] refusal'. Readers should treat r01-r30 as a 'steering bypass' of unclear sign. The original's capability-preservation part is not checked for attacked baselines.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests direction-based addition and removal effects on refusal, but does not establish that the direction is the sole mediator or that general capabilities are largely preserved after ablation.
No weight-edit or abliteration procedure is evaluated.
Tests direction-based ActAdd and ablation attacks, but not whether unrelated jailbreaks suppress this direction or whether training specifically against its ablation adds robustness.
Does not test whether refusal is carried by multiple directions, an affine structure, or a cone.
Does not distinguish harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
Does not test transfer across languages, base/instruct stages, or model variants of the same family.
Does not test how different refusal-training procedures or timing determine whether a removable direction exists.

relationships.condition: Directional ablation on all three baseline models and three harmful benchmarks; ActAdd bypass and induction on Llama2-7B-Chat and Qwen2-7B-Instruct
relationships.reason: Ablation drops refusal to 0.00-0.17 from 0.92-0.99 (r07, r09, r11, r19, r21, r23, r31, r33, r35). ActAdd drops harmful refusal to 0.01-0.14 (r01, r03, r05, r25, r27, r29) and induces harmless refusal of 1.00 and 0.91 (r37, r39).
relationships.display_finding: Ablation reduced refusal from 0.92–0.99 to 0.00–0.17, while additive steering reduced harmful refusal to 0.01–0.14 and induced harmless refusal of 1.00 and 0.91.

relation.reason: Although this is a defense paper, it reports refusal rates for the direction attacks on unmodified models, and those rates bear on V1.

tranche.reason: It reruns the Arditi et al. procedure on three unmodified models: difference-in-means direction, all-layer/all-position ablation and ActAdd (B.1, B.2). It uses the same measures: refusal substrings and Llama Guard 2 safety on 100 JailbreakBench prompts, plus 100 Alpaca prompts. It reports those attack results directly (Tables 1, 11, 12).

source_check.notes: The text names the harmful-prompt attack ActAdd and describes it as x<-x+r on harmless inputs (B.1), yet refusal falls; the bypass sign is never stated. The record omits Qwen2-0.5B-Instruct under ActAdd (Table 15: harmful refusal 0.01, benign refusal 0.91, no unattacked baseline). Rows are linked to V3 but have no V3 verdict; the defended and FT-model robustness results in Table 12 are not recorded.

statements.correction: Ablation refusal is 0.00-0.17 on JailbreakBench, AdvBench and HarmBench; unattacked baselines 0.92-0.99 are given for JailbreakBench only (Table 11). ActAdd harmful refusal is 0.01-0.14 on Llama2/Qwen2; harmless refusal is 1.00 and 0.91 (Table 1). Text has no random-direction control. Attacked-baseline values have no +/- (only FT/FJLT/Bottleneck models do). No capability benchmark is run on ablated or ActAdd models; the only measure is benign-response PPL under ActAdd (1.12->1.58, 1.27->1.72, 1.44->1.77). Code: supplementary material. A fourth model, Qwen2-0.5B-Instruct, gets ActAdd only (Table 15): harmful refusal 0.01, benign refusal 0.91.
statements.problem: All of this study's numbers are correct. The 'why' flags overstate the evidence. There is no random or orthogonal direction control. Attacked baseline values carry no uncertainty. The utility benchmarks (Table 13) cover only unattacked and defended models.

statements.correction: arXiv:2507.20333 has no random or orthogonal direction control. Its only comparisons are unattacked models (Table 11) and the authors' fine-tuned or defended models. Ablation 0.92-0.99 -> 0.00-0.17 and induced harmless refusal of 1.00 (Llama2) and 0.91 (Qwen2) are correct.
statements.problem: Numbers are right, but this study is listed as an example of results with a random or orthogonal control. It has none.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Directional ablation on the tested baseline chat/instruct models and harmful-prompt benchmarks
reader_labels.reason: Refusal scores are very low after the study’s all-layer/all-position directional ablation across the three tested models and benchmarks (r07, r09, r11, r19, r21, r23, r31, r33, r35). ActAdd also yields high benign-prompt refusal on Llama2 and Qwen2 (r37, r39). These results support intervention effects, but do not establish sole mediation or preserved general capability.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: ActAdd reduces harmful-prompt refusal less completely on Gemma than on the other tested baselines, with scores of 0.41, 0.39, and 0.36 across the three benchmarks (r13, r15, r17).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: ActAdd on harmless Alpaca prompts for Gemma-1.1-7B-IT
reader_labels.reason: Benign-prompt refusal rises to 0.62, a substantial but incomplete induction relative to the other tested models (r38).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: ActAdd and directional-ablation attacks on the tested baseline chat/instruct models
reader_labels.reason: The direction-based attacks generally yield low refusal and safety scores on harmful prompts across benchmarks, showing that these attacks can bypass refusal; the ActAdd results are less complete on Gemma (r01-r06, r13-r18, r25-r30, r07-r12, r19-r24, r31-r36).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Compared with Llama2 and Qwen2, Gemma retains higher refusal and safety scores after ActAdd across the reported benchmarks (r13-r18).
